# Non-Inferiority Trials {#sec-non-inferiority-trials}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Learning objectives"}
- Identify the non-inferiority margin and signed effect.
- Read the relevant confidence-interval boundary.
:::

## The idea

A non-inferiority trial seeks to rule out a prespecified, unacceptably large loss of benefit, rather than to prove treatments identical. If larger responses are favourable and $\Delta=effect_{new}-effect_{control}$, a commonly used convention sets the lower non-inferiority boundary at $-M$. The non-inferiority claim requires the appropriate one-sided lower confidence bound to exceed $-M$ under the prespecified framework.

## When and how to apply it

The margin must be justified clinically and, when an active control is involved, with relevant historical evidence and assumptions. Prespecify whether lower or higher values indicate benefit. Non-inferiority requires careful consideration of estimand, adherence and analysis populations.

## Teaching case 1 — baseline draft

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Clinical scenario / initial worked example"}
New versus standard treatment has a hypothetical margin of five percentage points on a higher-is-better recovery proportion. Label the unacceptable region below -0.05 and interpret intervals that cross the margin.
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Common error"}
A confidence interval that includes zero can still be compatible with non-inferiority; an interval crossing the non-inferiority margin does not establish it.
:::

## Hands-on exercise

Compare three hypothetical confidence intervals with the same margin: (-0.04,0.02), (-0.07,0.01), (0.01,0.06). Which support non-inferiority? Explain.

## Key message

Non-inferiority requires ruling out unacceptable harm against a justified margin.
